concept.name: Hexagonal Architecture

relationships.description: Connects Hexagonal Architecture to system design hld architectures in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core domain logic inside an explicit boundary where all external I/O—HTTP, SQL, queues, third-party APIs—plugs in through interfaces owned by the domain.
spark.keyTakeaway: By inverting dependencies so adapters depend on domain ports (never the reverse), you can swap databases, frameworks, or message brokers and run full business-logic tests in milliseconds with zero infrastructure.

concept.whyItMatters: In traditional layered architectures (`Controller -> Service -> Repository -> DB`), business rules inevitably leak framework annotations (`@Entity`, `@Transactional`, HTTP status codes) and SQL row shapes. When you need to support a Kafka consumer alongside REST, swap Stripe for Adyen, or migrate from DynamoDB to Postgres, every service method breaks. Hexagonal Architecture places the domain model at the center with zero external imports, forcing all I/O to translate at the edge.
whenToUse: Core business domains with complex invariants (billing, order state machines, risk scoring, ledger accounting) that outlive web frameworks and databases.
Systems with multiple entry points (REST API, gRPC, CLI, Kafka consumer) driving the exact same use cases.
Teams that want fast, deterministic unit tests for 90% of business rules without spinning up Docker/Testcontainers on every save.
whenNotToUse: Thin CRUD microservices or admin back-offices with almost no domain logic beyond validating JSON and writing rows.
Data-intensive ETL or reporting pipelines where SQL window functions and bulk set operations *are* the business logic; forcing them through domain objects kills performance.
Early-stage prototypes or hackathons where speed of iteration matters more than 5-year maintainability.
keyPoints: Driving (Primary) Ports are interfaces exposed *by* the application core (e.g., `PlaceOrderUseCase`), invoked by Driving Adapters (REST controller, gRPC handler, Kafka listener).
Driven (Secondary) Ports are interfaces defined *by* the core for what it needs (e.g., `OrderRepository`, `PaymentGateway`), implemented by Driven Adapters (Postgres, Stripe, in-memory fakes).

The Dependency Rule is strict and one-way: source-code imports only point inward (`adapters -> application -> domain`). The domain package has zero imports from Spring, FastAPI, Hibernate, or AWS SDKs.
Adapters own their own DTOs and ORM models (`OrderEntity`, `StripeChargeResponse`) and map them to/from pure domain entities (`Order`, `Money`) at the boundary.
Architectural fitness functions (ArchUnit in Java, `import-linter` in Python, `depguard` in Go) enforce the boundary automatically in CI so convenience imports don't erode it over time.

examples.title: Multi-channel order placement (REST + Kafka)
examples.scenario: An e-commerce checkout service accepts synchronous orders via `POST /v1/orders` and asynchronous subscription renewals from a `billing.renewals` Kafka topic.
examples.outcome: Both the Spring `OrderRestController` and `RenewalKafkaConsumer` (driving adapters) call the same `PlaceOrderPort.execute(PlaceOrderCommand)` use case. Validation, inventory reservation, and idempotency rules live once in the core, and swapping Postgres for an in-memory `FakeOrderRepository` lets the test suite run 400 domain tests in 120 ms.

examples.title: Anti-Corruption Layer (ACL) for a legacy ERP
examples.scenario: A modern fulfillment service must query a 15-year-old SOAP ERP that uses cryptic 3-letter status codes (`X9`, `P2`) and nullable XML strings.
examples.outcome: The `ErpInventoryAdapter` implements the clean `StockLookupPort` interface and translates `X9` -> `StockStatus.BACKORDERED` inside the adapter. No legacy ERP terminology ever enters the fulfillment domain model.

tradeOffs.pro: Domain logic is 100% decoupled from frameworks, enabling sub-second in-memory tests and painless major framework upgrades.
tradeOffs.con: Requires extra interfaces, mappers, and package structure—creating boilerplate for simple pass-through operations.

tradeOffs.pro: ORM lazy-loading bugs, JSON serialization quirks, and DB column renames stay trapped inside adapters.
tradeOffs.con: Converting `OrderEntity <-> Order <-> OrderResponseDto` adds repetitive mapping code and minor allocation overhead on high-throughput paths.

tradeOffs.pro: Core use cases stay explicit about consistency boundaries (e.g., via a `UnitOfWork` port).
tradeOffs.con: Without care, hiding persistence behind a `Repository` port can accidentally split one logical unit of work into multiple autocommit queries.

failureModes.name: Leaky ORM abstractions
failureModes.description: Putting `@Entity`, `@Column`, or SQLAlchemy `Base` directly on domain classes so `OrderRepository` returns framework-tracked proxies, causing `LazyInitializationException` in the domain.
failureModes.mitigation: Keep domain models as plain POJOs/dataclasses/structs and map from separate ORM entities inside the persistence adapter.

failureModes.name: Anemic pass-through boilerplate
failureModes.description: Every single `GET /users/{id}` query is wrapped in a `GetUserPort`, `GetUserUseCase`, `UserReadRepository`, and 4 identical DTOs with zero logic.
failureModes.mitigation: Apply CQRS pragmatically: use full Hexagonal ports for commands/writes with invariants, and allow thin read-only query handlers to project directly from the DB.

failureModes.name: Boundary erosion via shared utility imports
failureModes.description: A developer imports `org.springframework.http.HttpStatus` or `sqlalchemy.exc.IntegrityError` inside a domain service for convenience.
failureModes.mitigation: Add an automated CI check (ArchUnit / `import-linter` / Go `depguard`) that fails the build if `domain` imports any adapter or framework package.

failureModes.name: Mock-heavy tests drifting from real SQL behavior
failureModes.description: All tests run against an in-memory `HashMap` fake repository, passing in CI while production fails on a Postgres unique constraint or `NULL` handling.
failureModes.mitigation: Run a shared **contract test suite** against both the in-memory fake (every save) and the real Postgres/Kafka adapter via Testcontainers (in CI).

commonMistakes: Putting business logic inside driving adapters (controllers) or driven adapters (SQL queries / stored procedures) instead of the domain.
Naming ports after the technology (`PostgresOrderPort`, `KafkaEventPort`) instead of the domain intent (`OrderRepository`, `OrderEventPublisher`).
Returning HTTP status codes or framework exceptions from use cases instead of domain-specific result types or exceptions.
Splitting a single transaction across two repository calls without a `UnitOfWork` / transaction boundary port.
Enforcing 1-to-1 interface-per-class ceremony everywhere instead of reserving ports for genuine I/O boundaries.

sections.content:
## The idea

Proposed by Alistair Cockburn in 2005, **Hexagonal Architecture** (formally **Ports and Adapters**) reframes an application from a vertical stack (`UI -> Logic -> DB`) into an **inside/outside** symmetry. The **inside** (the hexagon) contains only pure domain entities, value objects, and application use cases. The **outside** contains every external actor: web browsers, gRPC callers, cron jobs, relational databases, Redis caches, and third-party webhooks.

Nothing outside touches the inside directly. Instead, the core defines **Ports** (technology-agnostic interfaces): **Driving Ports** on the left (what the app *offers*) and **Driven Ports** on the right (what the app *needs*). **Adapters** live strictly outside the hexagon, translating external protocols (HTTP JSON, SQL rows, Protobuf) into domain calls and back.

## Concrete walkthrough

Trace a `TransferFunds` use case in a banking service:

1. **Driving Adapter (`RestTransferController`)**: Receives `POST /v1/transfers` with `{ "from": "acc_1", "to": "acc_2", "cents": 5000 }`, validates HTTP headers/JWT, maps JSON into a `TransferCommand`, and calls the driving port `TransferFundsPort.execute(cmd)`.
2. **Application Core (`TransferFundsService`)**: Runs inside a `UnitOfWork` port. It loads `Account` aggregates via the driven port `AccountRepository.findById(...)`, calls `fromAccount.debit(Money.usd(5000))` and `toAccount.credit(...)` (enforcing overdraft invariants in pure domain code), saves both accounts, and emits `FundsTransferredEvent` through `DomainEventPublisher`.
3. **Driven Adapters**:
   - `PostgresAccountAdapter` implements `AccountRepository`, mapping `Account` domain objects to `accounts_tbl` rows via `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`.
   - `OutboxEventAdapter` implements `DomainEventPublisher`, writing the event to an `outbox` table in the same SQL transaction.
4. **Unit Test Swap**: In `TransferFundsTest`, `PostgresAccountAdapter` is replaced with `InMemoryAccountRepository`. Zero Spring context, zero Docker, and zero network calls—testing overdraft rules and double-entry balance invariants in < 1 ms.

data.title: Ports & Adapters dependency inversion flow

edges.label: Calls Driving Port
edges.title: Translate external input
edges.description: REST or Kafka adapter converts JSON/bytes into a `Command` and invokes the driving port.

edges.label: Enforce invariants
edges.title: Execute pure domain logic
edges.description: Domain entities validate business rules with zero framework or DB imports.

edges.label: Invokes Repository Port
edges.title: Dependency-inverted persistence
edges.description: Core calls `AccountRepository` interface; Postgres adapter implements it and maps rows.

edges.label: Invokes Gateway / Event Port
edges.title: Emit events or call external APIs
edges.description: Core calls `PaymentGateway` or `EventPublisher` port; adapter handles HTTP/ACL.

edges.label: Returns Domain Result
edges.title: Map outcome to protocol
edges.description: Driving adapter maps domain result or error to HTTP 201/422 or Kafka ack.

data.caption: All source-code dependencies point inward toward the hexagon; driven adapters implement interfaces owned by the core via Dependency Inversion.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Driving vs. driven ports and transaction boundaries
sections.content:
## Driving vs. driven ports and transaction boundaries

A frequent point of confusion is **who owns the interface**. In Hexagonal Architecture, the **core owns both**:

- **Driving Ports** (e.g., `PlaceOrderUseCase`) are *implemented by* the application service and *called by* controllers or CLI runners.
- **Driven Ports** (e.g., `OrderRepository`) are *called by* the application service and *implemented by* infrastructure adapters.

Because the core cannot import `@Transactional` without violating the dependency rule, model atomicity explicitly using a **`TransactionPort`** (or `UnitOfWork` closure: `tx.run(() -> { ... })`) implemented by the persistence adapter, or keep `@Transactional` in a thin application-wiring layer outside the pure domain entities.

## Architecture pattern comparison

| Dimension | Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) | Traditional 3-Tier Layered | Clean / Onion Architecture |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Dependency direction** | Outside -> Inside (via DIP) | Top -> Down (`Controller -> Service -> DB`) | Outer rings -> Inner rings (concentric) |
| **Primary boundary** | Inside (Core) vs. Outside (I/O) | Horizontal technical layers | Enterprise rules -> App rules -> Adapters |
| **Domain isolation** | Zero framework/DB imports | ORM `@Entity` often shared across all tiers | Zero framework/DB imports |
| **Test speed** | < 1 ms per use case with fakes | Slow (often requires DB/Spring test context) | < 1 ms per use case with fakes |
| **Best fit** | Long-lived domain services, multi-channel I/O | Simple CRUD APIs, rapid prototypes | Large enterprise domains with strict layering |

## Failure modes

- **God-port proliferation**: Defining a single `DatabasePort` with 40 methods forces every test fake to stub 40 methods. Keep driven ports small and cohesive (Interface Segregation Principle, e.g., `OrderReader`, `OrderWriter`).
- **Adapter logic creep**: Putting discount calculations inside a REST controller or eligibility filters inside a SQL `WHERE` clause splits business truth across tiers.
- **Fake-vs-Prod divergence**: In-memory fakes that don't enforce unique keys, transaction isolation, or pagination sorting create false confidence. Always pair fakes with a shared **Repository Contract Test** run against real Postgres in CI.
- **Over-mapping simple reads**: Running complex read dashboards through aggregate hydration (`N` entities + mappers) causes severe latency; bypass domain aggregates for read-only CQRS projections.

## Enforcing boundaries with fitness functions

Architecture diagrams rot unless automated tests enforce them. Add a build-time dependency check in CI:

- **Java / Kotlin**: Use **ArchUnit** (`noClasses().that().resideInAPackage("..domain..").should().dependOnClassesThat().resideInAnyPackage("..adapter..", "org.springframework..", "jakarta.persistence..")`).
- **Python**: Use **`import-linter`** contracts (`type = forbidden`) forbidding `domain` from importing `fastapi`, `sqlalchemy`, or `boto3`.
- **Go**: Place `domain` in an internal package and enforce import rules with **`depguard`** in `golangci-lint`.

Pair this with a **contract test suite**: an abstract test class verifying `save()`, `findById()`, optimistic locking, and not-found behavior, executed against both `InMemoryOrderRepo` and `TestcontainersPostgresOrderRepo`.

## Practical checklist

- [ ] Verify `domain` and `application` packages have zero imports from web frameworks, ORMs, or cloud SDKs.
- [ ] Name ports after domain capabilities (`PaymentGateway`, `OrderRepository`), not vendor implementations (`StripeClient`, `PostgresRepo`).
- [ ] Keep ORM entities and JSON DTOs inside `adapter` packages and map them explicitly at the boundary.
- [ ] Enforce package dependency rules automatically in CI using ArchUnit, `import-linter`, or `depguard`.
- [ ] Run a shared contract test suite against both in-memory fakes (fast unit loop) and real Testcontainers adapters (CI).
- [ ] Use thin read-only query projections (CQRS) for complex reporting endpoints instead of forcing them through domain aggregates.

interviewProblems.title: Hexagonal Architecture
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Hexagonal Architecture. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: Hexagonal Architecture (Ports & Adapters) isolates core domain logic inside an explicit boundary where all external I/O—HTTP, SQL, queues, third-party APIs—plugs in through interfaces owned by the domain.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Driven DB Adapter applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Driven External Adapter.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Driven External Adapter experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Keep domain models as plain POJOs/dataclasses/structs and map from separate ORM entities inside the persistence adapter.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: By inverting dependencies so adapters depend on domain ports (never the reverse), you can swap databases, frameworks, or message brokers and run full business-logic tests in milliseconds with zero infrastructure.
Avoid trap: Putting business logic inside driving adapters (controllers) or driven adapters (SQL queries / stored procedures) instead of the domain.
Avoid trap: Naming ports after the technology (`PostgresOrderPort`, `KafkaEventPort`) instead of the domain intent (`OrderRepository`, `OrderEventPublisher`).
When to reach for it: Core business domains with complex invariants (billing, order state machines, risk scoring, ledger accounting) that outlive web frameworks and databases.
When to reach for it: Systems with multiple entry points (REST API, gRPC, CLI, Kafka consumer) driving the exact same use cases.

putItTogether.title: Putting Hexagonal Architecture Together
putItTogether.summary: By inverting dependencies so adapters depend on domain ports (never the reverse), you can swap databases, frameworks, or message brokers and run full business-logic tests in milliseconds with zero infrastructure.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Hexagonal Architecture before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Both the Spring `OrderRestController` and `RenewalKafkaConsumer` (driving adapters) call the same `PlaceOrderPort.execute(PlaceOrderCommand)` use case. Validation, inventory reservation, and idempotency rules live once in the core, and swapping Postgres for an in-memory `FakeOrderRepository` lets the test suite run 400 domain tests in 120 ms.
